bat-removal.intro: Union's bat colonies hold the historic county seat's tall attics — the pre-war and Victorian-era homes around the courthouse and along the old mill streets, in a Union County landscape of rolling piedmont, creeks, and the Tyger River to the south. Big brown bats are the usual tenants, feeding over the creeks and the town's canopy and returning to roof voids that have stood undisturbed above quiet houses for generations of summers. Union's older housing presents the classic entry list — failed gable screens, fascia joints, chimney flashing, the junctions of a century of additions — and the colonies use it thoroughly.
bat-removal.extendedBody:
The county-seat roofline, read completely

Union's exclusions succeed or fail on the mapping. A historic roofline here offers a colony several exits, and sealing the one the homeowner noticed merely promotes the second. We find the active entries by staining and the evening flight, fit one-way devices when the timing allows, and seal every remaining gap in the same programme — metal and screen fitted to old framing, chimney caps as a matter of course. The timing follows SCDNR's guidance: South Carolina has no statutory bat season, but no competent operator seals a maternity colony while the pups cannot fly; a colony mapped in June is excluded in the proper window, priced once and held. Bats need no permit in this state. What they need is a roofline with no way back in, and on a Union historic home that is a carpenter's list, executed completely, once.

faqs.q: How much does bat removal cost in Union?
faqs.a: It depends on the colony and the entry count — Union's historic homes run to several entries across their layered rooflines, and completeness is the variable that decides whether the job is done once. We inspect and map first, then quote the full exclusion with all secondary sealing included, firmly, before work starts. Colonies found during the pup season are mapped at the first visit and excluded in their window at the quoted price, so the calendar never becomes a second bill.

faqs.q: We keep finding single bats in our Union home in late summer. Is that the attic colony?
faqs.a: Usually it is the colony's young. Late summer is dispersal, when the year's pups are flying and inexperienced ones turn up in living spaces, stairwells, and chimneys. A single indoor bat is handled the same day — close the room, keep people and pets clear, and call; if it was in a room where someone slept, SC DPH reporting is part of the process and we manage it with you. But treat the strays as the colony's advertisement: the attic needs mapping and a scheduled exclusion, because next summer's strays are already born.

snake-removal.intro: Lockhart is a Broad River mill town — a small Union County community built where the river bends, with its mill-era housing on the slopes above the water and the river bottoms at its feet. Its snake work is river work: watersnakes and racers along the banks and in the bottoms, rat snakes in the mill cottages' crawlspaces and the older homes, and copperheads in the rocky, wooded slopes between the town and the river — the Lockhart slopes, with their stone, leaf litter, and sun-warmed edges, are classic copperhead ground. The river also delivers the seasonal pattern: high water pushes the bottomland snakes up into the town's low yards, and the calls follow the river's level as much as the calendar.
snake-removal.extendedBody:
The bluff, the bottoms, and the flood line

Lockhart snake work starts with the water. After high river, the bottoms' population — watersnakes mostly, harmless and displaced — turns up in the low yards and crawlspaces, and most of those animals leave when the water does; we identify them and say so. The established calls are the slope dwellers: copperheads in the stone and litter between the houses and the river, removed when they have taken up at a home's ground — its woodpile, its porch void, its garden wall. And the mill cottages carry the rat snake pattern: a climbing, nonvenomous snake in a crawlspace is hunting rodents, and its removal includes the rodent read, because evicting the snake while keeping its food supply is a subscription. In a town this size, we also teach the map: which banks and slopes hold the copperheads, which bottoms hold only watersnakes, so the knowledge stays on the street after the truck leaves.

faqs.q: The Broad River flooded and now there are snakes in our Lockhart yard. Are they dangerous?
faqs.a: Most flood-displaced snakes here are watersnakes — nonvenomous, unsettled, and temporary; they follow the water back down as it falls. Copperheads are the exception to respect, and they come from the slopes, not the flood. Keep dogs and children out of the low yard until the water is down, photograph anything you are unsure of from a distance, and send it to us — identification is free. A snake that stays after the water leaves, or any snake under the house, is a visit; a snake passing through a flooded yard is weather, and we will tell you the difference honestly.

faqs.q: How much does snake removal cost in Lockhart?
faqs.a: It depends on the species and the search — a located rat snake in a crawlspace is compact; a copperhead in a slope garden takes finding. Photograph first, from a safe distance: identification is free and settles a large share of calls with no visit needed. Removals are quoted before we come, and every removal visit includes the habitat read — woodpiles, porch voids, rodent sign — because in Lockhart the snake is always the second sentence of the story.

squirrel-removal.intro: Jonesville is a small Union County town with a textile past — a compact community of mill-era and older homes in the rolling piedmont, where the Pacolet River runs to the east and farm and timber country presses every edge. Its gray squirrels work the town's mature street canopy and the big oaks in the older yards, denning in the attics of the pre-war homes and chewing in at the mill cottages' repeated roof details. Jonesville's housing was built in rows and eras, and its squirrel entries repeat with the floor plans: the same eave detail, the same gable vent, street after street — which makes the pattern easy to read and the sealing, done once in metal, easy to keep.
squirrel-removal.extendedBody:
The repeating detail, sealed in metal

A Jonesville squirrel job starts with identification: which era of house, which roof detail failed. Mill-era cottages concentrate their risk in a few junctions, and squirrels — which learn details rather than addresses — work the pattern across a street. We exclude the colony with one-way devices, then rebuild the failed detail in metal that outlasts the original material, and check the rest of the roofline for the same detail in its early stages. The attic gets its own read: nesting in the insulation, the beginnings of wiring damage, and the droppings that say how many seasons the colony has been in residence. On the town's older individual homes the read is the full historic one — layered junctions, chimney flashing, porch-roof meetings — because those entries are one-offs and have to be found one by one. Either way the principle in Jonesville is the county's usual one: the animal comes out under the rules, and the metal is what makes it a finished job instead of a season's truce.

faqs.q: How much does squirrel removal cost in Jonesville?
faqs.a: It depends on the house — a mill cottage with one failed eave detail is a compact job; a larger older home with several junctions in play is more. We inspect the whole roofline, name the detail that failed, and quote the exclusion and metal sealing firmly before work begins. The written note names the detail plainly, which matters on Jonesville's repeating streets: the same detail is on your neighbours' houses, and they will want to know.

faqs.q: Squirrels chewed our Jonesville wiring. How serious is that?
faqs.a: Serious enough to be the reason squirrel jobs should not wait. Chewed insulation on attic wiring is a genuine fire risk — it is the damage we check for first in any colony of more than a few weeks, and we document what we find for you and, if it is needed, for an electrician. The squirrels themselves are excluded and the entries sealed; the wiring is a separate repair we will flag honestly and never inflate. If we find active damage to conductors, we will tell you to have it looked at before the circuit is trusted, in those words.
